h1: Splitting one batch to compare two dry hops
title: Split One Batch to Compare Dry Hops | Craft Beer School
desc: How to split a fermented homebrew into two vessels, dry hop each with a different hop and compare them fairly without oxidising the beer.
teaser: Hop descriptions all sound the same. Dry hop one beer two ways and you will taste the real difference.
standfirst: A split dry hop is the cleanest way to learn what a hop variety actually smells like in beer. One base beer, two vessels, two hops. The hard part is moving fermented beer without letting oxygen ruin both halves.
sections: Why split at the dry hop stage

Hop catalogues describe nearly everything as citrus, tropical or pine. In the glass, two hops with the same words on the packet can smell completely different. The only reliable way to learn them is to taste them in the same beer, side by side.

Splitting at the dry hop stage keeps everything upstream identical. Same mash, same boil, same yeast, same fermentation. The only change is the hop that goes in at the end, so every difference in aroma belongs to that hop. It also costs very little extra: one brew day, a second vessel and two small packets of hops.
Brew a base beer that gets out of the way

The base beer should be a quiet canvas. A pale ale of about 1.045 to 1.050 with pale malt, a little wheat or carapils for body and a clean bittering charge to around 25 to 30 IBU works well. Skip late kettle hops, or keep them small, so the dry hop has the stage to itself.

Ferment with a clean ale yeast at 18 to 20 °C. Fruity English strains add esters that blur the hop aroma. Kveik can work in a hot kitchen, but pick one of the cleaner strains.

You have two choices. Split the wort into two fermenters on brew day and dry hop each one later, or ferment in one vessel and split near the end. Splitting on brew day is simpler and keeps oxygen out, because the beer never moves after fermentation. If you only own one big fermenter, split when fermentation is nearly finished.

The danger in moving beer is oxygen. Oxygen picked up after fermentation dulls hop aroma within days and turns hoppy pale beers darker and sweeter in flavour. Transfer through a tube that sits at the bottom of the receiving vessel, never splashing. If you have a CO2 cylinder, purge each vessel first. Splitting while a little fermentation is still running helps too: the yeast uses up some of the oxygen you pick up.

Our guide to brewing a hazy IPA without it turning brown goes deeper on oxygen control at home.

Keep the dose identical by weight in each half. For a test, around 4 to 5 grams per litre gives a clear aroma without wasting hops; that is 40 to 50 grams in each 10 litre half. Weigh on a kitchen scale, not by the scoop.

Dry hop at fermentation temperature, around 18 to 20 °C, for two to four days. Longer contact rarely adds much aroma and can pull out grassy, vegetal notes. Add both hops on the same day and package both on the same day.

One thing to watch: hops contain enzymes that can break down some of the sugars the yeast left behind. Fermentation can restart quietly after dry hopping, which brewers call hop creep. Check the gravity before you bottle. If it has dropped since you split, give the beer a few more days or you risk overcarbonated bottles.

Bottle or keg both halves the same day, with the same priming sugar per litre and the same conditioning temperature. Label them clearly. Store both cold once carbonated, because warm storage strips hop aroma fast. In an Indian summer, a week in a cupboard at 32 °C can take a hoppy beer from bright to dull. The fridge is your friend here.

Taste them young. Dry hop aroma is at its best within two to four weeks of packaging.

Pour both into identical glasses at the same temperature, around 8 to 10 °C. Have someone else pour and mark the glasses underneath so you do not know which is which. Smell before you taste and write your first impression in plain words: lime peel, mango, cut grass, onion, resin. Then taste for bitterness, because some hops add a harsher edge than others even when dry hopped.

Swap the order on a second round. The first glass often seems stronger simply because your nose was fresh. A triangle test, three glasses with one odd one out, tells you whether you can really tell them apart.
Build a hop library one split at a time

Keep notes on every split in one place: the hops, the dose, the days of contact and what you smelt. After five or six splits you will have a personal hop library based on your own beer, which is worth more than any catalogue. Pair it with a split yeast batch and you will start to see how much of a beer's aroma comes from each.

Describing aroma precisely and consistently is a skill that can be trained, just as tasting faults can. Most brewers never train it formally.

Your first step: choose two hops you keep reading about, buy a 50 gram packet of each and plan a split on your next pale ale.
faqs: How much dry hop should I use in a test batch?
About 4 to 5 grams per litre gives a clear aroma for comparison. Use the same weight in each half.
How long should I dry hop for?
Two to four days at fermentation temperature is enough for most hops. Longer contact can bring out grassy, vegetal notes.
Enzymes in hops can break down leftover sugars so fermentation restarts after dry hopping. Check the gravity before bottling to avoid overcarbonation.
How do I stop oxygen ruining a split batch?
Split on brew day if you can. Otherwise transfer gently through a tube at the bottom of the vessel, purge with CO2 if you have it and split while fermentation is still slightly active.
